rows.speaker: القاضي أبو يعلى
rows.claim: He argues that a living Khidr would attend Friday prayer, congregational prayer, and jihad with Muhammad; a living Moses would have had to follow Muhammad, and Jesus will pray behind this community's imam.
rows.anchor: وكيف يعقل وجود الخضر ولا يصلي مع رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم الجمعة والجماعة ولا يشهد معه الجهاد

rows.speaker: القاضي أبو يعلى
rows.claim: If Khidr were Adam's direct son, his age would exceed six thousand years; if an early descendant, he should be immense, but alleged witnesses report no giant stature.
rows.anchor: أنه يلزم أن يكون عمره اليوم ستة آلاف سنة أو أكثر

rows.speaker: القاضي أبو يعلى
rows.claim: The report that Adam was sixty cubits tall and human stature diminished afterward also conflicts with claims that Khidr was an early descendant but ordinary-sized.
rows.anchor: خلق آدم طوله ستون ذراعا فلم يزل الخلق ينقص بعده

rows.speaker: القاضي أبو يعلى
rows.claim: If Khidr lived before Noah, he should have boarded the Ark, yet no report says that he did.
rows.anchor: لو كان الخضر قبل نوح عليه السلام لركب معه في السفينة ولم ينقل هذا أحد

rows.speaker: القاضي أبو يعلى
rows.claim: Scholars agree that Noah and those with him died after leaving the Ark, leaving only his descendants, as the verse says.
rows.anchor: العلماء اتفقوا على أن نوحا عليه السلام لما خرج من السفينة مات ومن معه

rows.speaker: القاضي أبو يعلى
rows.claim: A human surviving from Adam until near the world's end would be a major sign and should have been mentioned, as Noah's 950 years were.
rows.anchor: لو صح بقاء بشر من لدن آدم إلى قرب خراب الدنيا لكان ذلك من أعظم الآيات

rows.speaker: القاضي أبو يعلى
rows.claim: Claiming Khidr lives without Quran, Sunna, or binding consensus is speaking about God without knowledge, which the Quran forbids.
rows.anchor: القول بحياة الخضر قول على الله تعالى بغير علم وهو حرام بنص القرآن

rows.speaker: القاضي أبو يعلى
rows.claim: Anecdotes of sightings cannot establish identity: alleged witnesses have no reliable sign distinguishing Khidr from someone falsely claiming to be him.
rows.anchor: هل للخضر علامة يعرفه بها من رآه وكثير من زاعمي رؤيته يغتر بقوله أنا الخضر

rows.speaker: القاضي أبو يعلى
rows.claim: It is implausible that Khidr left Moses, saying they must part, only to associate with ignorant people who neglect Islamic practice and claim his counsel.
rows.anchor: يفارق الكليم ويدور على صحبة جاهل لا يصحبه إلا شيطان رجيم

rows.speaker: القاضي أبو يعلى
rows.claim: The community would not accept a claimant Khidr's report from the Prophet; saying he never met or was not sent to the Prophet would itself entail grave unbelief.
rows.anchor: لو قال : سمعت رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم يقول : كذا وكذا لم يلتفت إلى قوله

rows.speaker: القاضي أبو يعلى
rows.claim: If alive, Khidr should serve Islam through jihad, prayer, and teaching rather than wander among wild animals in deserts.
rows.anchor: لكان جهاده الكفار ورباطه في سبيل الله تعالى ومقامه في الصف ساعة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The report that Khidr would visit the Prophet if alive is fabricated and has no basis, according to hadith critics.
rows.anchor: خبر لو كان الخضر حيا لزارني وهو كما قال الحفاظ خبر موضوع لا أصل له

rows.speaker: النووي
rows.claim: Al-Nawawi reports that the majority of scholars hold Khidr alive and present among people, a position agreed upon among Sufis.
rows.anchor: وذهب جمهور العلماءإلى أنه حي موجود بين أظهرنا وذلك متفق عليه عند الصوفية قدست أسرارهم

rows.speaker: الثعلبي
rows.claim: Al-Tha'labi describes Khidr as a long-lived prophet, hidden from most people's sight.
rows.anchor: أن الخضر نبي معمر على جميع الأقوال محجوب عن أبصار أكثر الرجال

rows.speaker: ابن الصلاح
rows.claim: Ibn al-Salah says Khidr remains alive today with the majority of scholars and ordinary people; some hadith scholars deny this.
rows.anchor: هو حي اليوم عند جماهير العلماء والعامة معهم في ذلك وإنما ذهب إلى إنكار حياته بعض المحدثين

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: A report transmitted by al-Daraqutni and Ibn Asakir says Khidr is Adam's direct son and his life was extended until he deceives the Antichrist; the author says this is not mere opinion.
rows.anchor: الخضر ابن آدم لصلبه ونسيء له في أجله حتى يكذب الدجال ومثله لا يقال من قبل الرأي

rows.speaker: ابن إسحق
rows.claim: Ibn Ishaq reports that Adam asked Noah's sons to bury his body in Syria and that Khidr eventually buried him, earning prolonged life; the author calls this explanation remote and notes the better-known water-of-life account.
rows.anchor: أن الخضر هو الذي تولى دفنه فأنجز الله تعالى له ما وعده

rows.speaker: علي
rows.claim: A report says Ali met a man at the Kaaba who identified himself as Khidr and promised forgiveness for a devotional supplication after obligatory prayer.
rows.anchor: والذي نفس الخضر بيده وكان هو الخضر لا يقولن عبد دبر الصلاة المكتوبة

rows.speaker: علي
rows.claim: In a report from Ibn Abbas, Ali says Khidr attended Muhammad's funeral and corrected a voice that had urged them not to wash the Prophet, identifying that voice as Satan.
rows.anchor: قال : أنا الخضر حضرت جنازة محمد صلى الله عليه وسلم

rows.speaker: جابر
rows.claim: Al-Hakim reports from Jabir that a dignified stranger consoled the Companions after Muhammad's death; Abu Bakr and Ali identified him as Khidr.
rows.anchor: فقال أبو بكر وعلي رضي الله تعالى عنهما : هذا الخضر عليه السلام

rows.speaker: ابن عساكر
rows.claim: Ibn Asakir reports that Khidr and Ilyas fast Ramadan in Jerusalem, perform pilgrimage yearly, and drink Zamzam sufficient for a year.
rows.anchor: أن إلياس والخضر يصومان شهر رمضان في بيت المقدس ويحجان في كل سنة

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: A marfu report from Ibn Abbas says Khidr and Ilyas meet annually during pilgrimage, shave each other's heads, and part after reciting a formula of reliance on God.
rows.anchor: يلتقي الخضر وإلياس كل عام في الموسم فيحلق كل واحد منهما رأس صاحبه

rows.speaker: محمد بن المنكدر
rows.claim: A report says a mysterious man delayed Umar's funeral prayer, praised the deceased, vanished after burial, and left a cubit-long footprint; identifying him as Khidr is an inference, not explicit in the report.
rows.anchor: والاستدلال بهذا مبني على أنه عنى بالمحدث عنه الخضر عليه السلام

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Many reports establish at most that Khidr lived in Muhammad's era, which rebuts those denying life then but does not prove he is alive now; the author says no group accepts the former while denying the latter.
rows.anchor: وإن لم يدل على أنه حي اليوم بل يدل على أنه كان حيا في زمنه صلى الله عليه وسلم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Stories of pious Successors and Sufis meeting Khidr across the ages are too numerous and famous to count, though hadith scholars deny that he narrates from the Prophet.
rows.anchor: وحكايات الصالحين من التابعين والصوفية في الاجتماع به والأخذ عنه في سائر الأعصار أكثر من أن تحصر

rows.speaker: الشيخ علاء الدين
rows.claim: Unlike hadith scholars, Shaykh Ala al-Din claims to receive Prophetic hadith directly from Khidr without an intermediary.
rows.anchor: فقد ادعى الشيخ علاء الدين استفادة الأحاديث النبوية عنه بلا واسطة

rows.speaker: السهروردي
rows.claim: Al-Suhrawardi says Khidr narrated three hundred hadiths to them that he heard directly from the Prophet.
rows.anchor: أن الخضر عليه السلام حدثنا بثلثمائة حديث سمعه من النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم شفاها

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Those affirming Khidr's present life use continuity of a previously established state until contrary proof appears.
rows.anchor: بالاستصحاب فإنه قد تحققت من قبل بالدليل فتبقى على ذلك إلى أن يقوم الدليل على خلافها

rows.speaker: أنصار حياة الخضر
rows.claim: They answer the hundred-year hadith by saying it excludes Khidr only after a century, or that he was then over water; they also read its scope as people ordinarily seen, excluding angels and Satan.
rows.anchor: لا يوجب نفي حياته في زمانه صلى الله عليه وسلم وإنما يوجب لظاهره نفيها بعد مائة سنة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The hadith's apparent scope includes anyone ordinarily dwelling on earth, including someone at sea; excluding sea-dwellers would weaken its generality and would not decisively refute later long-lived claimants such as Ratan.
rows.anchor: على ظهر الأرض من هو من أهل الأرض ومتوطن فيها عرفا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The suggestion that Khidr was in the air when the hadith was spoken is weak; if alive, he should ordinarily be visible, and an exception needs proof.
rows.anchor: يرد على الجواب الثاني أن الخضر لو كان موجودا لكان ممن يشاهده الناس كما هو الأمر المعتاد في البشر

rows.speaker: أنصار حياة الخضر
rows.claim: They answer Ibn Taymiyya's objection that Khidr must have met the Prophet by citing believers such as Uways al-Qarni and Najashi who did not meet him; they suggest Khidr may have come secretly.
rows.anchor: فهذا خير التابعين أويس القرني رضي الله تعالى عنه لم يتيسر له الإتيان والمرافقة في الجهاد

rows.speaker: عبد الله بن المبارك
rows.claim: Ibn al-Mubarak recounts a battlefield encounter in which a handsome, fragrant man helped revive his dead horse; the story continues in the next segment.
rows.anchor: فوقع فرسي ميتا فرأيت رجلا حسن الوجه طيب الرائحة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Ibn al-Mubarak account explicitly places Khidr in a battle, and the author says the Prophet's Badr prayer meant Islam would cease to be publicly dominant if the company died, not that no believer existed elsewhere.
rows.anchor: فهذا صريح في أنه قد يحضر بعض المعارك وأما قوله صلى الله عليه وسلم اللهم إن تهلك هذه العصابة لا تعبد في الأرض

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The author rejects comparing Khidr to Uways or Najashi: all prophets followed Muhammad during the Ascension, and Khidr had no apparent barrier to meeting him; equating their status risks unbelief.
rows.anchor: ومتى زعم أحد أن نسبته إلى نبينا صلى الله عليه وسلم كنسبته إلى موسى عليه السلام فليجدد إسلامه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The claim that Khidr secretly learned from the Prophet for a divine wisdom lacks evidence; if this were so, he could have visited once or twice as Gabriel appeared in Dihya's form.
rows.anchor: على أنه لو كان كذلك لذكره صلى الله عليه وسلم ولو مرة وأين الدليل على الذكر

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The author dismisses the Ibn al-Mubarak story as unproven and implausible, saying Khidr's presence at the Prophet's command to Sa'd would matter more than appearing to Ibn al-Mubarak.
rows.anchor: وأما ما روي عن ابن المبارك فلا نسلم ثبوته عنه وأنت إذا أمعنت النظر في ألفاظ القصة استبعدت صحتها

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Badr hadith can support Khidr's absence; interpreting it to mean only that no one would visibly worship God fails because it repeats the unsupported claim that Khidr was unseen.
rows.anchor: فالاستدلال بالحديث على عدم وجود الخضر عليه السلام له وجه

rows.speaker: أنصار حياة الخضر
rows.claim: They answer the verse denying immortality by saying they do not claim Khidr is eternal: some say he will fight the Antichrist, die when the Quran is lifted, or die near the end times.
rows.anchor: بأن المراد من الخلد الدوام الأبدي والقائلون بوجوده اليوم لا يقولون بتأبيده

rows.speaker: الراغب
rows.claim: Al-Raghib says Arabic uses 'everlasting' for things that decay slowly, such as stone hearths; the author calls the response strong because Noah also lived long.
rows.anchor: كل ما يتباطأ عنه التغير والفساد تصفه العرب بالخلود كقولهم للأثافي خوالد

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Defenders say extraordinary age is no objection if Khidr's life is miraculous; early peoples were not always gigantic, and Khidr might have been granted Gabriel-like shape-changing power, though the author notes these replies are contestable.
rows.anchor: فبأن البعد العادي لا يضر القائل بتعميره هذه المدة المديدة لأن ذلك عنده من خرق العادات

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The author objects that reports of tiny Gog and Magog concern the end times and do not establish ancient stature; shape-changing for saints is disputed, and if granted to anyone the Prophet could have used it during the Hijra.
rows.anchor: وفي ثبوته للأولياء خلاف كثير من المحدثين

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Defenders say failure to report Khidr on Noah's Ark does not prove he was absent: he may have boarded unseen or avoided the water by becoming enormous or taking to the air; the author presents these as speculative counterarguments.
rows.anchor: لا يلزم من عدم نقل كونه في السفينة إن قلنا بأنه عليه السلام كان قبل نوح عليه السلام عدم وجوده

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A report attributed to al-Alami says Khidr guides lost sailors and Ilyas guides lost travelers in mountains, then both guard Gog and Magog's wall at night; a similar Anas report has a weak chain.
rows.anchor: أن الخضر يدور في البحار يهدي من ضل فيها وإلياس يدور في الجبال يهدي من ضل فيها

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Against the claim that only Noah's descendants survived the flood, defenders question whether all others died, read 'his descendants' as survival by reproduction rather than exclusivity, and note the devil was also aboard; the pre-Noah chronology is weak.
rows.anchor: لا نسلم الاتفاق على أنه مات كل أهل السفينة ولم يبق بعد الخروج منها غير نسل نوح عليه السلام

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Defenders say Khidr's long life need not appear in the Quran: Noah's lifespan consoles Muhammad about rejection by his people, while Khidr's story would not serve that purpose; mentioning Noah also implies longer life is possible.
rows.anchor: وإنما ذكر سبحانه نوحا عليه السلام تسلية لنبينا صلى الله عليه وسلم بما لاقى من قومه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The explicit mention of Noah's long life may imply that a longer life is possible, but it proves possibility rather than Khidr's actual survival.
rows.anchor: من ذكر طول عمر نوح عليه السلام تصريحا يفهم تجويز عمر أطول من ذلك تلويحا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A counterargument says Khidr's longevity is itself a sign of lordship that would fittingly balance the Quran's mention of long-lived Satan; mentioning it may also bring Muhammad joy.
rows.anchor: لا أقل من أن يذكر هذا الأمر العظيم في القرآن العظيم مرة لأنه من آيات الربوبية

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Some interpret God-given mercy in this verse as a hint that Khidr had a long life, but that reading presupposes the very view it is meant to prove.
rows.anchor: إشارة إلى طول عمره عليه السلام على ما سمعت عن بعض في تفسيره

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Defenders answer the fifth objection by saying Khidr's life is established by Sunna; Ibn al-Qayyim instead says every hadith about Khidr's life is false and challenges proponents to prove authenticity.
rows.anchor: إنا نختار أنه ثابت بالسنة وقد تقدم لك طرف منها

rows.speaker: ابن الصلاح
rows.claim: Proponents appeal to an alleged consensus of leading shaykhs and most scholars, which Ibn al-Salah, al-Nawawi, and others transmitted.
rows.anchor: وقد نقل هذا الإجماع ابن الصلاح والنووي وغيرهما

rows.speaker: صدر الدين إسحق القونوي
rows.claim: The author denies a Sufi consensus because al-Qunawi locates Khidr's existence in the imaginal realm, al-Kashani treats Khidr and Ilyas as spiritual states, and others call Khidriyya a rank held by righteous people.
rows.anchor: أن وجود الخضر عليه السلام في عالم المثال

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Even if a majority of scholars hold Khidr alive, that is not the binding legal consensus the opposing party demands; disputed Sufi interpretations also undermine claims of universal agreement.
rows.anchor: إجماع جماهير العلماء على ما نقل ابن الصلاح والنووي مسلم لكنه ليس الإجماع الذي هو أحد الأدلة الشرعية

rows.speaker: أنصار حياة الخضر
rows.claim: Defenders say Khidr has identifying signs, including greenery at his footsteps, a cubit-long foot, miracles, and popular claims about his thumb and a moving pupil; the author asks for proof of these signs.
rows.anchor: أن له علامات عند أهله ككون الأرض تخضر عند قدمه وأن طول قدمه ذراع

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The authentic report explains the name Khidr by greenery springing up where he sat; it does not make this a permanent sign, and the cubit-foot report is not authenticated.
rows.anchor: أنه إنما سمي الخضر لأنه جلس على فروة بيضاء فإذا هي تهتز من خلفه خضراء

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Changing appearances and miracles cannot prove a claimant is Khidr: saints may perform wonders, speak metaphorically as 'Khidr,' or use identity language as Sufis do; good opinion cannot yield certainty.
rows.anchor: وظهور الخوارق مشترك بينه وبين غيره من أولياء الأمة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The author rejects the claim that Khidr meets ignorant lawbreakers, attributing such stories to liars; the stronger claim is that he meets major ascetics who observe religious limits.
rows.anchor: فالكاذبون الدجالون يكذبون على الله تعالى وعلى رسوله صلى الله عليه وسلم

rows.speaker: علي الخواص
rows.claim: Ali al-Khawwas reportedly asked Khidr to accompany him on pilgrimage, but Khidr refused because reliance on his presence might weaken al-Khawwas's trust in God.
rows.anchor: وسئل عن سبب إبائه فقال : خفت من النقص في توكلي حيث اعتمد على وجوده معي

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The author says meetings with Khidr could be visions of sacred spirits appearing in forms, like reports that Muhammad saw Moses praying in his grave, in heaven, and circumambulating the Kaaba; Ibn Arabi also claims meetings with prophets and the unborn Mahdi.
rows.anchor: أن الأرواح المقدسة قد تظهر متشكلة ويجتمع بها الكاملون من العباد

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Because such apparitions and spiritual meetings remain possible, reported encounters do not establish that Khidr exists bodily among people as an ordinary human.
rows.anchor: ومع قيام هذا الاحتمال لا يحصل اليقين أيضا بأن الخضر المرئي في الخارج كوجود سائر الناس فيه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: One of the author's transmission routes for the Bashishiyya prayer passes through his teachers to Khidr, then to Abd al-Salam ibn Mashish.
rows.anchor: فإني أرويها من بعض الطرق عن شيخي علاء الدين علي أفندي الموصلي

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The author says denying that Muhammad was sent to Khidr need not be unbelief, though it is unanimously false; he proposes that Khidr came and pledged allegiance inwardly, unseen.
rows.anchor: ونختار أنه أتى وبايع لكن باطنا حيث لا يشعر به أحد

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Some scholars of legal theory counted Khidr among the Companions, but his reports were not accepted because his existence and presence at the encounter could not be established with certainty.
rows.anchor: وقد عده جماعة من أرباب الأصول في الصحابة ولعل عدم قبول روايته لعدم القطع في وجوده

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Defenders say a possessor of ladunni knowledge follows God's instruction for each place and time; the author replies that absence should be assumed until evidence establishes Khidr's presence.
rows.anchor: بأن النفي مستند إلى عدم الدليل فنحن نقول به إلى أن يقوم الدليل

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Shafi'i, al-Muzani, and al-Sayrafi accept istishab to affirm or deny a state previously established without contrary probability; Hanafis and theologians use it only defensively, not to prove Khidr's current life.
rows.anchor: وأما عندنا وكذا عند المتكلمين فهو من الحجج القاصرة التي لا تصلح للإثبالت وإنما تصلح للدفع

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The missing person inherits under the affirmative view but not under the Hanafi approach, since inheritance is an affirmative ruling; non-inheritance can instead be maintained defensively.
rows.anchor: فالمفقود يرث عنده لا عندنا لأن الإرث من باب الإثبات فلا يثبت به

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Ordinary custom makes survival through so many ages improbable, defeating istishab's condition that no contrary probability arise.
rows.anchor: فإن العادة قاضية بعدم بقاء الآدمي تلك المدة المديدة والأحقاب العديدة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Custom is meaningful evidence: without it, a miracle's breach of custom could not produce belief or compel following; even if custom does not prove death, it creates a probability against istishab.
rows.anchor: إن العادة دليل معتبر ولولا ذلك لم يؤثر خرق العادة بالمعجزة في وجوب الاعتقاد والاتباع

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The author says the reliable proof must come from Quran, Sunna, binding consensus, or analogy, and neither analogy nor the cited scripture, reports, or claimed consensus establish Khidr's present life.
rows.anchor: فالمعول عليه الخالص من شوب الكدر الاستدلال بأحد الأدلة الأربعة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: After weighing the evidence, the author says authentic Prophetic reports and strong rational premises favor Khidr's death; only deference to uncertain saintly stories and Sufi authorities pulls the other way.
rows.anchor: الأخبار الصحيحة النبوية والمقدمات الراجحة العقلية تساعد القائلين بوفاته عليه السلام

rows.speaker: ابن عربي
rows.claim: Ibn Arabi teaches that embodied messengers are the human world's poles and guardians, and that God preserved four messengers bodily after Muhammad's death: Idris, Ilyas, Jesus, and Khidr, though Khidr's inclusion is disputed outside their group.
rows.anchor: أبقى الله تعالى بعد وفاته عليه الصلاة والسلام من الرسل الأحياء بأجسادهم في هذه الدار أربعة إدريس وإلياس وعيسى والخضر

rows.speaker: ابن عربي
rows.claim: In Ibn Arabi's account, these surviving messengers hold the offices of spiritual stakes, imams, and pole, preserving faith, sainthood, prophecy, and messengership in the world until the Resurrection.
rows.anchor: وكلهم الأوتاد وإثنان منهم الأمامان وواحد منهم القطب

rows.speaker: ابن عربي
rows.claim: Ibn Arabi says Muhammad's leadership over the prophets during the Ascension showed his bodily leadership; after his death, the living messengers preserve the religion until God inherits the earth.
rows.anchor: فلهذا صلى صلى الله عليه وسلم ليلة الإسراء بالأنبياء عليهم السلام لتصح له الإمامة على الجميع

rows.speaker: ابن عربي
rows.claim: Ibn Arabi presents this account as a distinctive insight and says only spiritual deputies, not ordinary saints, know these hidden messengers and their role.
rows.anchor: وهذه نكتة فاعرف قدرها فإنك لا تراها في كلام أحد غيرنا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The account implies Khidr is a messenger, a view the author calls weak among most scholars; it also implies his life until Judgment, alongside Jesus, whose later marriage, children, death, and burial beside Muhammad are commonly reported.
rows.anchor: وعلم منه القول برسالة الخضر عليه السلام وهو قول مرجوح عند جمهور العلماء

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The author asks how Ibn Arabi can say Jesus remains on earth when Jesus, like Idris, is currently in heaven; readers should accept Khidr's life only if they accept such claims on authority rather than proof.
rows.anchor: ولينظر ما وجه قوله قدس سره بإبقاء عيسى عليه السلام في الأرض وهو اليوم في السماء كإدريس عليه السلام

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The author urges readers to assess both sides' evidence and recalls Ali's counsel to judge what is said rather than who says it, then follow one's considered judgment.
rows.anchor: لا تنظر إلى من قال وانظر ما قال فاستفت قلبك بعد الوقوف على أدلة الطرفين

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: He criticizes people who brand dissent from Sufi teachings as bad faith and quotes Sufi voices urging trust in the path; Abu Yazid says believers should ask such people to pray, while Abu Imran warns against rejecting claims unsupported by a contrary proof.
rows.anchor: يا أبا القاسم لا تفعل فإنك إن فعلت هذا جمعنا بين حرمانين

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The author concludes that claims rejected by sound religious or rational evidence should not be accepted, and asks God for guidance to what pleases Him.
rows.anchor: ويفهم منه أن ما يرده الدليل الشرعي أو العقلي لا يقبل وهو الذي أذهب وبه أقول

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The indefinite accusatives 'mercy' and 'knowledge' magnify both gifts; the knowledge is beyond comprehension, immeasurable, and concerns hidden secrets and the unseen.
rows.anchor: للتفخيم وكذا في قوله سبحانه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Some explain 'from Our presence' by saying knowledge is among God's most particular attributes; knowledge precedes will, and will precedes the exercise of power that brings things into existence.
rows.anchor: إن القدرة لا تتعلق بشيء ما لم تتعلق الإرادة وهي لا تتعلق ما لم يتعلق العلم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The phrase 'from Our presence,' especially before 'knowledge,' signals knowledge specially granted by God and known only through His enabling; 'We taught him' magnifies the teaching compared with 'We gave him.'
rows.anchor: تعظيم أمر هذا العلم ما فيه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The teaching may have come through audible angelic revelation, nonverbal angelic inspiration called nafth, or inspiration; Sufis posit an angel of inspiration for prophets and others and methods of perceiving the unseen through inner purification.
rows.anchor: وأن يكون بواسطة الوحي الحاصل بإشارة الملك من غير بيان بالكلام وهو القسم الثاني

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A hadith says the Holy Spirit breathed into the Prophet that no soul dies before completing its provision, urging people to fear God and seek provision graciously.
rows.anchor: إن روح القدس نفث في روعي أنه لن تموت نفس حتى تستكمل رزقها

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Sufis use this verse as a basis for ladunni knowledge, often called the knowledge of reality or inner knowledge, though some object to those labels.
rows.anchor: والآية عندهم أصل في إثبات العلم اللدني وشاع إطلاق علم الحقيقة والعلم الباطن عليه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The account resumes with Moses' question, prompted by the narrative, and his request is permission to follow Khidr on condition that Khidr teach him.
rows.anchor: استئناف مبني على سؤال نشأ من السياق كأنه قيل فما جرى بينهما من الكلام

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Alusi reads 'ala' in Moses' request as expressing a condition: jurists treat this use as literal, al-Sarakhsi says so, some grammarians omit it, and al-Subki questions its Arabic usage; Alusi considers it valid whether literal or figurative.
rows.anchor: والحق أنه استعمال صحيح يشهد به كتاب حقيقة كان أو مجازا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: 'Rushd' means attaining what is good; the accusative is chiefly an emphatic descriptor of the omitted second object of 'teach,' though other syntactic parses are possible and less apparent.
rows.anchor: أي علما ذا رشد وهو إصابة الخير

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Abu Amr, al-Hasan, al-Zuhri, Abu Bahriyya, Ibn Muhaysin, Ibn Munadhir, Yaqub, Abu Ubayd, and al-Yazidi read rushdan with fatḥ; most of the seven read rushdan with ḍamm and sukūn, both dialect forms.
rows.anchor: وقرأ أبو عمرو والحسن والزهري وأبو بحرية وابن محيصن

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The syntax can also take 'rushd' as a substitute for 'what you taught,' as the purpose of following, or as an implicit verbal noun; Alusi calls the first alternative less apparent.
rows.anchor: بدل منه وهو خلاف الظاهر وأن يكون

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Learning from Khidr does not compromise Moses' prophetic rank: a messenger need be most knowledgeable about doctrines of his own law, not every hidden or unseen subject, and can learn from another prophet.
rows.anchor: في العقائد ما يتعلق بشريعته لامطلقا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Some rejected that this Moses was the son of Imran because they thought a messenger must know more than everyone in every field; Alusi rejects that premise and compares learning specialized knowledge to jurists learning jafr from others.
rows.anchor: ومن هنا قال نوف وأضرابه : إن موسى هذا ليس هو ابن عمران

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A concern that unseen knowledge is not beneficial guidance cites the verse saying that knowledge of the unseen would yield more good and avert harm; Alusi also reports the view that Khidr was not sent to Moses' community and therefore could know what Moses did not.
rows.anchor: والخضر عليه السلام نبي لم يرسل إليه ولا هو مأمور باتباع شريعته فلا ينكر تفرده

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: One inference from the alternative view is that Khidr was not an Israelite, since Moses apparently was sent to all Israelites.
rows.anchor: أنه على هذا ليس الخضر عليه السلام من بني إسرائيل لأن الظاهر إرسال موسى عليه السلام إليهم جميعا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Alusi's own view is that Moses possessed knowledge of reality and inner or ladunni knowledge but Khidr knew more of it, while Moses knew more of outward religious law; each surpassed the other in one field.
rows.anchor: أن لموسى عليه السلام علما بعلم الحقيقة المسمى بالعلم الباطن والعلم اللدني إلا أن الخضر أعلم به منه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Calling Khidr more knowledgeable than Moses in the reports means more knowledgeable in some subject, not every subject; comparative adjectives can denote superiority in one domain, as with the verse about signs being greater than one another.
rows.anchor: ليس على معنى أنه أعلم منه من كل وجه بل على معنى أنه من بعض الوجوه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Alusi notes that 'more knowledgeable' can be restricted to a field, as one person may surpass another in medicine while the other excels in agriculture.
rows.anchor: زيد أعلم من عمرو في الطب وعمرو أعلم منه في الفلاحة

rows.speaker: الخضر
rows.claim: A hadith from Ibn Abbas in Bukhari, Muslim, Tirmidhi, and Nasa'i has Khidr tell Moses that God taught each of them knowledge unknown to the other, supporting their different areas of expertise.
rows.anchor: إني على علم من علم الله تعالى علمنيه لا تعلمه أنت وأنت على علم من علم الله تعالى علمك الله سبحانه لا أعلمه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Alusi identifies Khidr's distinctive knowledge as some knowledge of reality and Moses' as some religious law; both knew both domains, but differed in degree in their present circumstances.
rows.anchor: فلكل من موسى والخضر عليهما السلام علم بالشريعة والحقيقة إلا أن موسى عليه السلام أزيد بعلم الشريعة

rows.speaker: جلال الدين السيوطي
rows.claim: Al-Suyuti says only Muhammad combined reality and religious law; Alusi reads this as a claim about their fullest form, since every prophet has some share in the knowledge of sainthood.
rows.anchor: ما جمعت الحقيقة والشريعة إلا لنبينا صلى الله عليه وسلم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Alusi says Muhammad was uniquely commanded to convey both reality and law in their complete form, though the idea that he alone was commanded to convey reality to the prepared remains questionable.
rows.anchor: فإنه عليه الصلاة والسلام مأمور بتبليغ الحقيقة كما هو مأمور بتبليغ الشريعة

rows.speaker: علي الخواص
rows.claim: Al-Khawwas says prophetic knowledge follows the needs of each messenger's community, while as saints some messengers can possess more knowledge of sainthood than even the greatest messengers.
rows.anchor: العلم تابع للرسالة فإنه ليس عند كل رسول من العلم إلا بقدر ما تحتاج إليه أمته فقط

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Alusi considers prophets' knowledge of reality, as a form of sainthood, greater than that of nonprophet saints; he will not rank a nonprophet over Moses or affirm Khidr's sainthood while denying his prophethood.
rows.anchor: ولا تراني أفضل وليا ليس بنبي في علم الحقيقة على ولي هو نبي ولا أقول بولاية الخضر عليه السلام دون نبوته

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Those who call Khidr a saint but not a prophet seem committed to saying that he exceeded Moses in knowledge of reality; some instead deny that Moses had any such knowledge, without lowering his rank.
rows.anchor: وقائلو ذلك يلزمهم ظاهرا القول بأن ما عنده من علم الحقيقة مع كونه وليا أكثر مما عند موسى عليه السلام

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Alusi rejects the Sufi claim that sainthood as a whole outranks prophethood; he reports debate over whether a prophet's own sainthood or prophethood is superior and chooses prophethood.
rows.anchor: أن الولاية مطلقا أفضل من النبوة وإن كان الولي لا يبلغ درجة النبي وهو مردود عند المحققين بلا تردد

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Some mystics prefer a prophet's sainthood because it is not confined to a time as legislative prophecy is; Alusi chooses prophethood, and rejects the Karramiyya claim that a saint can equal or surpass a prophet.
rows.anchor: واختار هذا بعض العرفاء معللا له بأن نبوة التشريع متعلقة بمصلحة الوقت

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Moses' phrasing displays humility, courtesy, and gentleness toward Khidr despite his own exalted rank; Fakhr al-Din al-Razi counts twelve aspects of this courtesy.
rows.anchor: ما راعاه موسى عليه السلام في سوق كلامه على علو مقامه من غاية التواضع مع الخضر

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Khidr's 'indeed' and 'never' make the prediction emphatic; saying Moses will not be able to be patient, rather than simply will not be patient, denies the capacity required for the act.
rows.anchor: نفي لأن يصبر معه على أبلغ وجه حيث جيء بأن المفيدة للتأكيد وبلن

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The wording 'you will not be able' logically entails that patience will not occur, and the indefinite 'patience' under negation generalizes to no patience at all.
rows.anchor: في سياق النفي وذلك يفيد العموم اي لا تصبر معي أصلا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Khidr signals that he will do things whose outward appearance is objectionable and whose purpose Moses cannot know; even a righteous lawgiver will recoil, and Khidr knows Moses' sharp temper and zeal.
rows.anchor: يتولى أمورا خفية المراد منكرة الظواهر والرجل الصالح لا سيما صاحب الشريعة لا يتمالك أن يشمئز عند مشاهدتها

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: 'Khabran' is parsed as a specification transformed from a subject phrase ('what your knowledge did not encompass'), from the verb meaning to know; alternatively it is a cognate accusative because encompassing commonly means knowing.
rows.anchor: على التمييز المحول عن الفاعل والأصل ما لم يحط به خبرك

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-Hasan and Ibn Hurmuz read khubran with a damma on the bāʾ.
rows.anchor: وقرأ الحسن وابن هرمز ( خبرا ) بضم الباء

rows.speaker: الإمام
rows.claim: The Imam and others infer that capacity does not precede an act: if Moses already had capacity for patience, denying that capacity would be false, so it must arise only with the act.
rows.anchor: استدلوا بالآية كما قال الإمام وغيره على أن الاستطاعة لا تحصل قبل الفعل

rows.speaker: الجبائي
rows.claim: Al-Jubba'i answers that Khidr means patience would be burdensome, like colloquial claims that someone cannot bear seeing or sitting with another; the Imam objects that this departs from the apparent wording.
rows.anchor: بأن المراد من هذا القول أنه يثقل عليك الصبر كما يقال في العرف

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Alusi says the verse does not clearly prove that capacity cannot precede action: it denies patience by denying its prerequisite whether capacity is prior to or simultaneous with the act; al-Kurani says the earlier-capacity view also belongs to the Salaf.
rows.anchor: والإنصاف أن الاستدلال بها على ما ذكر غير ظاهر لأن المراد ليس إلا نفي الصبر بنفي ما يتوقف هو عليه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Moses promises that Khidr will find him patient if God wills and that he will not disobey; joining the verb to the participle can mean 'patient and not disobeying,' or it can coordinate with 'you will find me.'
rows.anchor: ستجدني إن شاء الله صابرا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: For the coordination, Alusi prefers construing 'I will not disobey' with 'patient,' yielding an accusative clause as a second complement of 'find'; the alternative attaches it to the main promise and has no syntactic case according to al-Zamakhshari.
rows.anchor: والظاهر الجواب الأول وأول الوجهين في العطف هو الأولى

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Treating the second clause as a direct continuation of Moses' quoted words answers the objection that it should also be in the accusative; the mention of God's will creates no difficulty if the promise is conditional.
rows.anchor: وذكر المشيئة إن كان للتعليق فلا إشكال في عدم تحقق ما وعد به
